\begin{abstract}
\textbf{Context.} A rapidly growing body of empirical work estimates how much of
open-source software is now written by AI, and a second body of work builds on those
estimates to argue about maintainer burden, contribution quality and project
sustainability. Nearly all of it rests on one of three measurement strategies:
zero-shot statistical detectors, heuristic phrase and formatting filters, or
large language models used as classifiers.
\textbf{Objective.} None of these instruments has been validated against ground truth
on open-source artifacts. They were benchmarked on news articles, student essays and
curated code benchmarks, not on commit messages, pull request descriptions, issue
reports or real-repository diffs. This paper inverts the prevailing question: instead
of measuring how much AI-generated content exists, it measures what the instruments
used to detect it actually detect.
\textbf{Method.} We assemble ground truth without human annotation. Agent-attributed
contributions from the AIDev dataset and \texttt{Co-authored-by} trailers provide a
high-precision positive set; artifacts written in the same repositories before the
public release of ChatGPT provide a negative set that is machine-generated-text-free by
construction. We evaluate \RESULT{n} detection approaches across five artifact genres,
stratified by agent, programming language, text length and project characteristics, and
propagate the measured error rates into corrected prevalence estimates.
\textbf{Results.} \RESULT{RQ1--RQ3 headline results}
\textbf{Conclusions.} \RESULT{conclusion}

\end{abstract}
